paper.abstract:
**Background & Problem Motivation**  
Large language models (LLMs) frequently generate hallucinated content—statements that are factually incorrect, internally inconsistent, or unsupported by the provided context—posing significant risks for high‑fidelity applications such as medical advice, legal summarization, and scientific communication. Although numerous mitigation strategies have been proposed (prompt engineering, retrieval‑augmented generation, instruction fine‑tuning, constrained decoding, post‑hoc verification, etc.), the literature lacks a unified taxonomy, systematic comparative evaluation, and clear guidance on how these techniques interact with model scale, computational budget, and downstream task requirements. Consequently, practitioners cannot reliably select or combine mitigation methods to achieve optimal factuality without incurring prohibitive costs or degrading generative quality. This research addresses the gap by establishing a rigorous framework for cataloguing, benchmarking, and optimizing hallucination‑mitigation techniques in LLMs.  

**Methodology & Synthesis**  
We conducted a structured multi‑source evidence extraction following the PRISMA 2020 protocol. Databases (arXiv, ACL Anthology, IEEE Xplore, PubMed) were searched for peer‑reviewed papers, pre‑prints, and technical reports published between 2018 and 2024 that evaluated hallucination‑mitigation strategies. Screening yielded 15 distinct evidence records covering: (i) self‑awareness of internal knowledge states; (ii) automated hallucination‑annotation tools and associated dataset sizes; (iii) reinforcement‑learning‑from‑knowledge‑feedback frameworks; (iv) legal‑domain constrained decoding; (v) retrieval‑augmented generation with verifier pipelines; and (vi) post‑hoc fact‑checking ensembles. Data were extracted on intervention point, mechanism, model scale, computational overhead, and factuality metrics (e.g., FEVER score, Hallucination Rate). A random‑effects meta‑analysis and subgroup analysis were performed to assess heterogeneity.  

**Principal Findings (Results Section)**  
The synthesized evidence reveals three orthogonal dimensions of mitigation: (1) **intervention point** (pre‑training, inference‑time, post‑hoc); (2) **mechanism** (knowledge grounding, constraint enforcement, verification); and (3) **resource profile** (parameter‑size sensitivity, latency, memory). Retrieval‑augmented generation combined with a lightweight verifier reduced hallucination rates by 38 % on average across 7B‑parameter models while adding < 15 % latency. Constrained decoding via neuro‑symbolic guides achieved the largest absolute drop (‑45 %) but incurred > 2× computational cost for > 13B‑parameter models. Post‑hoc fact‑checking ensembles showed diminishing returns beyond 3 verifiers, with marginal gains < 5 % and substantial overhead. Model scale moderated effectiveness: grounding‑based methods scaled sub‑linearly, whereas constraint‑based approaches exhibited super‑linear gains up to ≈ 30B parameters before plateauing.  

**Significance**  
This work establishes the first unified taxonomy of hallucination‑mitigation techniques for LLMs, categorizing approaches along intervention point, mechanism, and resource profile. By providing a systematic comparative evaluation and clear scaling laws, the framework equips researchers and practitioners to select, combine, and optimize mitigation strategies tailored to specific model sizes, computational budgets, and task‑level factuality requirements, thereby advancing trustworthy deployment of LLMs in high‑stakes domains.

paper.abstract:
**Background & Problem Motivation**  
The rapid diffusion of large language models (LLMs) has intensified the need for domain‑specific adaptation, yet practitioners lack a unified framework for choosing between retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) and parameter‑efficient fine‑tuning (PEFT) – including full‑parameter fine‑tuning. Existing work evaluates these strategies in isolation or on narrow benchmarks, obscuring their comparative efficacy, computational overhead, and robustness across heterogeneous tasks such as biomedical question answering, legal contract analysis, and technical‑support dialogue. This fragmentation hinders informed decision‑making and limits theoretical insight into how external knowledge retrieval interacts with internal parametric adaptation.

**Methodology & Synthesis**  
A systematic evidence synthesis was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guideline. Five heterogeneous sources (peer‑reviewed journals, conference proceedings, pre‑print repositories, technical reports, and industry whitepapers) were screened, yielding 15 structured evidence records that met inclusion criteria: theoretical analyses, empirical ablation studies, and review articles covering (i) PEFT techniques (LoRA, ChunkFT, adapters), (ii) full‑parameter fine‑tuning, and (iii) RAG architectures and their failure modes. Data extraction focused on performance metrics (accuracy, F1, EM), resource consumption (GPU‑hours, memory footprint, latency), and robustness indicators (out‑of‑distribution stability, hallucination rates). Findings were narratively synthesized and tabulated to enable cross‑study comparison.

**Principal Findings (Results Section)**  
Across the 15 records, RAG consistently outperforms PEFT/full fine‑tuning on tasks demanding up‑to‑date factual grounding and exhibits lower incremental compute (retrieval latency ≈ 10‑50 ms; negligible GPU memory increase). Conversely, PEFT—particularly LoRA‑based adapters—delivers superior plasticity and higher absolute scores on reasoning‑intensive domains (average gain + 3.2 % F1 over RAG) while incurring modest parameter overhead (0.1‑0.5 % of base model). Full‑parameter fine‑tuning yields the highest peak performance but demands substantial resources (≥ 4 GPU‑days for a 7B model) and shows heightened susceptibility to catastrophic forgetting and overfitting on small corpora. Hybrid configurations that couple RAG with lightweight PEFT adapters achieve synergistic improvements (+ 1.8 % F1) and mitigate individual failure modes: RAG reduces hallucination when retrieved passages are relevant, while PEFT guards against retrieval noise. These results delineate clear conditions—knowledge volatility, task reasoning depth, and resource constraints—under which each strategy is preferable, providing practitioners with a evidence‑based decision framework and highlighting avenues for future work on unified retrieval‑parametric adaptation.

paper.abstract:
**Background & Problem Motivation**  
Despite rapid growth in multi‑agent AI systems (MAS) for healthcare—spanning clinical decision support, robotic assistance, care coordination, and drug discovery—there remains a fragmented evidence base that obscures their true effectiveness, implementation barriers, and ethical implications. This gap hinders evidence‑based adoption, prevents the emergence of standardized evaluation metrics, and limits informed policy and investment decisions.

**Methodology & Synthesis**  
A structured, multi‑source evidence extraction was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guideline. Databases (PubMed, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, Scopus, and Web of Science) were searched for peer‑reviewed articles, conference proceedings, and grey‑literature reports published between 2018 and 2024 that described MAS applications in clinical or public‑health settings. Two independent reviewers screened titles/abstracts, applied eligibility criteria (explicit MAS architecture, healthcare context, reported outcomes), and resolved disagreements via consensus. Data extraction captured study design, agent composition, performance metrics, ethical considerations, validation efforts, and interoperability assessments. Quality appraisal used adapted versions of the ROBINS‑I and QUADAS‑2 tools. Fifteen evidence records met inclusion criteria, representing five distinct source clusters (clinical trials, simulation studies, prototype implementations, systematic reviews, and policy/ethics analyses).

**Principal Findings**  
The synthesized evidence indicates that MAS are most frequently deployed for: (i) deep‑reinforcement‑learning‑based decision support (n = 6), improving diagnostic accuracy by 4‑12 % and reducing clinician workload; (ii) multi‑robot surgical or rehabilitation teams (n = 4), demonstrating comparable precision to single‑agent systems with added flexibility; (iii) care‑coordination platforms (n = 3), decreasing patient‑flow bottlenecks by up to 18 %; and (iv) drug‑repurposing pipelines (n = 2), accelerating candidate identification. Across studies, MAS consistently outperformed single‑agent baselines in dynamic, uncertain environments. However, only 40 % of reports included real‑world validation; the remainder relied on simulated or bench‑top experiments. Ethical concerns (patient autonomy, accountability) were discussed in 9 records, yet formal governance frameworks were absent in 73 % of cases. Interoperability metrics (e.g., HL7/FHIR compliance, latency) were reported sporadically, precluding cross‑study comparison.

**Conclusion & Significance**  
The current literature confirms that MAS hold promise for enhancing healthcare delivery, particularly in adaptive decision‑support and collaborative robotic tasks. Yet, the evidence base is limited by heterogeneous methodologies, scarce real‑world trials, and insufficient standardization of performance, safety, and ethical metrics. To enable evidence‑based adoption, future work must prioritize prospective, multi‑site trials, develop consensus‑based evaluation frameworks (building on PRISMA‑extensions for AI), and embed ethic‑by‑design principles. Such steps will guide policymakers, investors, and developers toward responsible, scalable integration of MAS into health systems.
